# Week 1 Article Review:

## An evaluation of mapped species distribution models used for conservation planning. 

Authors: @Johnson2005

### Background

-   Researchers compare the performance of species distribution models
    (SDMs) using four different modeling techniques: Habitat suitability
    index (HSI), logistic regression-based resource selection function
    (RSF), Mahalanobis distance, and an ecological niche model.

    -   HSI applies expert knowledge and meta-analysis to rank
        wildlife-habitat relationships using additive, multilplicative
        or logical variables with coefficients typically ranging from 0
        to 1 based on percieved relevance.

    -   RSF was defined as "any mathematical funciton that provides
        predictions of resource or habitat use taht are proportional to
        the true probabliltiiy of use." The model is based on the theory
        that when use of habitat exceeds availability, then selection is
        inferred, and when use is lesss than availability then the
        habitat is avoided.

    -   Mahalanobis distance is described as a multivariate
        dissimiliarity statistic. In the context of SDMs, the mean
        conditions of a set of environmental variables are compared to
        other locations around the broader landscape. When a larger
        value of the statistic represents a larger deviation from the
        mean conditions.

    -   Ecological niche models are explicityly linked ot niche theory,
        and are used to represent species distribution across larger
        scale regions. These models seem to require much more indepth
        knowledge about the studied species as the model relies on
        evolutionary constructs that determine whether a set of
        environmental variables can or cannot support a species
        population.

-   To evaluate performance, they measuered differences in the
    distribution of ranked habitats, and they evaluated the predictive
    ability of the occurence of habitats that correlated with known
    species locations.

### Methods

-   The authors selected models based on relevance (i.e. contemporary
    and proad usee in existing literature), ability to be used within
    GIS, and representation of the data types necessary to parameterize
    models.

    -   The HSI was based on preivous reasearch and was derived from
        published literature, agencyt reports and expert opinion. The
        index was then ranked on a six class scale: high, moderately
        high, moderate, low, very low, and nil.

    -   The RSF was based on fixed-effects logistic regression:
        $$ w(x) = exp(\beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 + ... + \beta_nx_n) $$
        where $\beta_1...\beta_n$ are coefficients generated from the
        regrfession and $w(x)$ is the relative probablility of species
        occurance.

    -   Mahalanobis distance was calculated at each raster cell using
        GIS using the formula: $$D^2 = (x-m)^TC^{-1}(x-m)$$ where $D^2$
        is th eMahalanobis distance, $x$ is the habitat variable, $m$ is
        the mean value of habitat characteristics recorded at known
        locations, $T$ indicates that vector should be transposed, and
        $C^{-1}$ is the covariance matrix for the same vector of habitat
        characteristics. The authors used ESRI ArcView and GIS IDRISI to
        perform matrix calculations on ecological variables.

    -   The ecological niche model was adobted from teh Genetic
        Algorithm for Rule_set Prediction (GARP) computational approach
        for modeling. The GARP model is a standalone machine-learning
        process that develops rule sets to best identify species
        distribution.

-   For the RSF, Mahalanobis distance, and niche model, the authors
    developed 3 sets of models for each. The HSI model was predetermined
    via previous research. A total of 10 maps were created and
    normalized by calculating number of species locations within each of
    6 habitat classes.

-   Relationship between predicted class and normalized frequency of
    species locations were evaluated using Spearman rank and Pearson
    correlations. Kappa index of agreement was used to measure spatial
    correlation between maps.

-   Using the results of the correlations, the authors evaluated only
    the maps for each model that demonstrated the highest predictive
    ability.

### Key Findings

-   There was no reported significance in predictive capability between
    different variable sets or quantitative models. Comparing
    quantitative to qualitative models, the maps generated with HSI had
    weakest correlation and underperformed relative to other techniques.

-   Of the models, Mahalanobis distance was best at preicitng
    high-quality habitat, followed by RSF and niche models. Conversely,
    HSI was poor at predicting high-quality habitat. All models
    performed well at predicting low-quality habitat.

-   Modeling technique largely dertermined by data availability and
    costs. RSFs provide greatest flexibility as model parameters are
    easily assessed. Mhalanobis distancs and niche models do not provide
    metrics for evaluating strength of variable relationships. HSI
    coefficients are difficult to evaluate.

### Significance

-   Author's demonstrate that there is a benefit to using quantitative
    models over qualitative models when evaluating species distribution.
    But acknowledge, that the choice of modeling technique should be
    based on data availability and costs. Further, this paper
    demonstrates that there is value in using multiple modeling
    techniques to compare the effectiveness for SDM.

### Relevance to Capstone and Final Thoughts

-   This paper largely employs the same thesis that my project would be
    based around. I think there could be some potential using the same
    approach to evaluate Oyster habitat in the Pensacola Bay area.

-   While this paper is very helpful in guideing my thoughts on my own
    research, I Will keep searching for more recent papers that have
    used similar approaches to evaluate species distribution as this one
    is from 2005.

-   The author's cite a number of research papers that aim to compare
    model performance in SDM that would prove beneficial to review.

# Week 2 Article Review:

## Estuary-Specific and Adaptive Habitat Suitability Index Model for the Eastern Oyster Crassostrea Virginica in the Pensacola Bay System, Florida, USA

Authors: @Geselbracht2024

### Background

The paper opens with discussion on the sharp decline in geographic distribution of the Eastern Oyster Crassostrea virginica in recent decades. The authors attribute the decline to anthropogenic influences such as un-sustainable management policies, overharvestings, mining of oystershell as construction material, shifting hydrology, water quality degradation, siltation and sedimentation, diseaase and predation, erosion. As a result, the decline in *C. virginica* has also led to a decline in the many ecological and economical goods-and-services provided by healthy oyster reefs. Many ecological services were cited including: food production, fish and invertabrate habitat, shoreline protections, water filtration, and nutrient cycling. Declining oyster populations also produce negative economic impacts as the oyster related businesses and employment in fisheriees, recreation and the tourism industry begin to decline. 

The authors move on to discuss the decline within the context of the Pensacola Bay System (PBS) located in Pensacola, FL. The authors cite that the decline in oyster populations has been well documented in the PBS,citing that a historical US Fish Commission map depicts approximately 15,000ha of oyster reef in the system, and with more recent assessments found only 91.5ha. If accurate, this represents a 99.4% decline in oyster reef habitat in the PBS. Recognizing the sharp decline in oyster populations in the PBS, recent effort has been made to begin restoring oyster reefs in the system. However, the authors note that restoring such a large system is challenging. The authors cited a lack of information on system-specific characteristics, out of-date data, insufficient data coverage, and high monetary costs as barriers to successful restoration. To address these challenges, The Nature Conservancy (TNC) led a broad-based stakeholder engagement effort creating a Stakeholder Working Group (SWG) to develop an Oyster Fissheries and Habitat Management Plan. The SWG included represntatives from many backgrounds including: federal and state agencies, local governments, universities, non-governmental organizations, and the private sector. As part of the management plan, it was recogonized that determining where to prioritize restoration activities would in itself be quite challenging. This recogniztion led to to the development of a Habitat Suitability Index Model (HSI) for the PBS. 

The authors describe HSIs as decision support tools that can assis with the iedentification of areas to focus restoration efforts by integrating spatial information important to the survival of a particular species or habitat including biological, chemical, and/or physical characteristics. They also note that scocio-economic and regulatory information can also be incorporated into the model to factor in cost-benefit and or expediancy of restoration efforts. HSIs are described as being first developed by the US Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) in the 1980s and have been widely used for the eastern oyster throughout the United States and within the Gulf of Mexico region. While HSIs were orginally developed to determine species presence, they can also be used to determine where activities are likely to have greatest success. Factors included in the HSI are selected based on the purpose of the application, relying on data relevancy, availability, and quality. These factors are then weighted with scores ranging from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating greater suitability.

Finally, the authors describe the objectives of the study are as follows:

 1. to describe the devleopment of an estuary-specific decision support tool that streamlines the selection of restoration sites where restoration activities are likely to have the greatest success, even where data are limited, and

 2. to demonstrate the value of engaging resource knowledgeable stakeholders and resource users in the HSI development process, and 

 3. to illustrate how an HSI can be adapted as higher resolution data becomes available. 

The authors then hypothesize that "applying estuary specific and adaptable HSIs will streamline decisions regarding distribution of finite restoration funds to priority locations, prevent years of misguided work, and capitalize on remaining larval oyster sources in estuaries where reefs with live oysters have been greatly diminished."

### Methods

The study opted to leverage Geographic Information Systems (GIS) to develop the HSI model, following similar other models developed for oysters and other living marine organisms. Potential data sources were collated and the selected factors were evaluated for 1) availability, quality, and resolution of spatial extent, 2) relevance of the biological, chemical, and physical factors that indicate positive influence on oyster survival and reef formation without causing negative external effects, and 3) whether the factors repreented preexisting human uses that would conflict with restoration efforts. 

Through the study's review of available literature and stakeholder knowledge, 22 factors were identified as potentially import to oyster reef viability: aquaculture and shellfish leases, bathymetry, summer mean bottom dissolved oxgen (DO), chlorophyll a concentration, coastal maintained channels, contemporary oyster reef, disease intensity and prevalence, historical oyster reef presence, hydrology, oyster recruitment, managed areas, marsh migration areas, military zones, predation, regulatory restrictions, summer mean salinity, seagrass presence, sea level rise, shoreline type, substrate type, temperature, and water quality. Of these 22 factors, only 7 were selected for the model: contemporary oyster reef, summer mean bottom DO, historical oyster reefs, and oyster recruitment. The selected factors were each assigned as score between 0 to 1, with 1 representing optimal conditions and 0 representing unacceptable conditions. Depending on the factor type, the scoring was assigned as binary (0 or 1), grouped into bins based on a range of values, or assigned a dummy value based on qualitative characteristics. GIS was then used to convert each factor into a raster dataset spanning the PBS with a resolution of $124 m^2$, which was determined as an appropriate middle ground balancing the needs of stakeholder activity with computation processing time. One factor, oyster recruitment, required regularized spline interpolation using the mean recruits per shell per day over the study period. The resulting raster was a smooth gradient of estimated oyster recruitment over the entire PBS that was then standardized to have values of 0 to 1 for use in the HSI model. Finally, a composite score was calculated for the entire PBS using the following formula:

$$ 
Composite \  Score = \frac{({Factor \  Score}_1 + {Factor \  Score}_2 + ... + {Factor \  Score}_7)}{Max \  Score} 
$$

The resulting model was then reviewed during numerous meetings with members of the SWG to refine factor values to eventually generate the final model. 

### Key Findings

The resulting HSI was a raster grid covering the entire PBS with suitability values raging from 0.12 to 1.00. Using GIS the raster grid cells were then reclassified into 5 classes using natural breaks. The areas of highest suitability (score 0.74 to 1.00) represented 16% of the area with high (0.64 to 0.74), medium (0.54 to 0.64), low (0.41 to 0.53), and lowest (0.12 to 0.41) representing 27%, 20%, 20%, and 9%, respectively. 

Suitability scores were validated using digitized maps representing known oyster reef locations provided by local experts and oyster fishermen, in which there was agreement of 87% in areas with HSI scores > 0.50. Suggesting HSIs are a reliable tool for predicting species habitat and as a result, predict habitat suitability. 

### Significance

- The author's demonstrated that HSIs are useful in developing decision support tools when looking to determining where to prioritize ecosystem resotration efforts. Further, they demonstrated how quickly a model can be adjusted and re-run once developed, as they demonstrated when updating bottom sediment data from a study that was completed during the course of this research. The results of this study was able to help restoration practitioners greatly reduce the area of consideration by 57% for areas with an $HSI \ge 0.64$ and by 84% for areas with an $HSI \ge 0.74$. 

- The author's demonstrate that reliable HSIs can be built even when the study area may be lacking in high resolution input data, and that lack of quantitative data can be supplemented by expert knowledge. 

- The author's also suggest that the model can be adapted and used to predict future conditions by using climate change forcasts and future estimates. 

- The author's list their own key contributions as:
  1. Development of a relatively quick, simple and low-cost mehtod for developing a reliable HSI where quantitative physical and biological data for the system may be lacking in spatial or temporal resolution,

  2. illustrating the value of incorporating local expert nknowledge as an independent source of information to validate the HSI results,

  3. demonstrating how, once developed, the HSI can be relatively easily updated and adjusted to incorporate new or updated data as it becomes available. 

### Relevance to Capstone and Final Thoughts

This study is relevant because it will be used as the comparative analysis to my species distribution model. The authors have provided an accurate model that was validated using local expert knowledge. Further, it highlights the importance and need for generating quick and affordable suitability models that can be used to determine and prioritize restoration activities. Where this study relied on input from local stakeholders, my own project will remove the human element and look to demonstrate that a completely data driven approach is feasible rather than incorporating potential bias and hueristic processes that may arise when relying on human input. 

Additionally, where the author's of this study found a lack of spatial and temporal data I hope to incorporate spatial interpolation techniques using the largely available water quality data from the EPA's Water Quality Portal and the associated dataRetrieval package which can demonstrate a repeateable workflow that can provide updated outputs as more data is made available over time.
